full_text:
United Nations 
 
Nations Unies 
Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs 
 
The mission of the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) is to coordinate the global emergency response 
to save lives and protect people in humanitarian crises. We advocate for effective and principled humanitarian action by all, for all. 
www.unocha.org 
 
Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs 
 and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher 
Statement on El Niño 
El Niño is back. 
Extreme heat, droughts and floods are once again set to devastate communities across Latin 
America, Eastern and Southern Africa, Asia and the Pacific. 
The last El Niño in 2023-24 left tens of millions of people in need of food, nutrition, water, 
sanitation, health, agricultural support and protection. 
The forecasts are clear: this one looks even worse. It comes on top of widespread conflict, rising 
numbers of people on the move, and as soaring fuel, fertilizer and food prices are squeezing the 
most vulnerable families – while the humanitarian system reels from deep cuts. 
We are ready to disburse up to US$100m from the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) 
to get ahead of this El Niño. 
In support of that response, we are planning, implementing the lessons from the past, innovating, 
coordinating the humanitarian community and taking action. Our preparations are shaped by 
more sophisticated forecasts. More than $20 million has already been allocated for anticipatory 
action in six countries. Through CERF's Climate Action Account, we are investing in vulnerable 
communities to better withstand the climate shocks ahead. 
We need early, flexible financing – more effective and less costly in the long run – to match the 
scale of the risk. We ask for the world to prioritize conflict resolution and support to 
communities forced to flee. And we urge braver climate action in place of the short term and 
selfish decisions that are pushing us relentlessly towards the 1.5°C warming cliff edge. 
The choice is clear: we can wait for disaster, or we can invest in resilience. 
 
13 July 2026

Overview The Iran–United States crisis in 2026 has evolved from a high-intensity conflict into a fragile and uncertain de-escalation phase, but its global repercussions remain significant and ongoing.

These shocks are particularly severe for energy-importing and developing economies, contributing to slower global growth, higher food and commodity prices, and increased economic vulnerability across Asia.

Myanmar faces especially deep impacts due to its heavy dependence on imported fuel (around 9095% of supply), limited reserves, and fragile economic conditions; the crisis has led to rising fuel prices, shortages, currency depreciation, and increased costs of transportation, food, and agricultural production.

As a result, the conflict is not only a geopolitical issue but also a major economic shock, disproportionately affecting vulnerable countries like Myanmar, where it intensifies inflation, threatens livelihoods, and exacerbates existing economic instability.

related.title: How the United States and Iran Can Solve Hormuz
related.summary: As they jockey to strengthen their hand over the Strait of Hormuz, they risk a larger war that might include Israeli strikes on critical Iranian infrastructure and Houthi attacks in the Red Sea, effectively closing another major shipping route. In the early days of the April cease-fire, Iran declared the strait “completely open” to all commercial shipping through a “coordinated route,” signaling it would lift the de facto tolls imposed during the war and ease passage.
